\chapter{Friend, Family, Brother, and Sister}
\label{ch:pa-friend-and-family}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a friend, a family, a brother, and a sister in Punjabi, split \pa{ਪਰਿਵਾਰ} into its two Sanskrit pieces, and hear the same low tone open both \pa{ਭਰਾ} and \pa{ਭੈਣ} even though only one of the two is truly a cousin of its English counterpart.}

The chapter closes on \pa{ਭੈਣ}, said pàiṇ with the same initial-bh-to-low-tone shift as \pa{ਭਰਾ}: the reader produces \pa{ਦੋਸਤ}, \pa{ਪਰਿਵਾਰ}, \pa{ਭਰਾ} and \pa{ਭੈਣ}, states that \pa{ਭਰਾ} is the unbroken PIE cousin of brother while \pa{ਭੈਣ} descends from bhaginī and is NOT a cousin of sister, and names the tone rule's low-tone, word-initial case for the first time on a noun rather than a verb.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dost]{\pa{ਦੋਸਤ} — the one you chose}

\label{lesson:PA-C11-dost}



\begin{quote}
Four things you can ask for — \textbf{pāṇī}, \textbf{cāh}, \textbf{dudh}, \textbf{roṭī}. This chapter turns from things to people, starting with the one Chapter 2's \textbf{\pa{ਤੂੰ}} was really for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਦੋਸਤ}} — \emph{dost} — \textbf{friend}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਦ}} \emph{d}, \textbf{\pa{ੋ}} the \emph{o} sign, \textbf{\pa{ਸ}} \emph{s}, \textbf{\pa{ਤ}} \emph{t}. Every letter already yours, from \textbf{\pa{ਦੋ}}, \textquotedblleft{}two,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\pa{ਸਤਿ}}, \textquotedblleft{}truth.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਦੋਸਤ}} is \textbf{Persian}, not Sanskrit — borrowed from Classical Persian \textbf{dōst}, from Old Persian \textbf{dauštā}. Its root is Proto-Indo-European, meaning roughly \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to taste, to choose}.\textquotedblright{} Latin took the taste sense and left English \textbf{gusto} and \textbf{disgust}, both through \emph{gustare}. Germanic took the choosing sense and left Old English \emph{cēosan}, modern English \textbf{choose}. Persian took a third path: the \textquotedblleft{}chosen\textquotedblright{} one became the word for a friend.

So \textbf{dost} sits beside \textbf{roṭī} as this book's second honest gap: \textbf{roṭī}'s own root is lost to time; \textbf{dost}'s is not lost, but it belongs to Persian, not to the Sanskrit line most of your nouns so far have followed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{dost} — friend
  \item \emph{Trace it:} PIE \textquotedblleft{}taste, choose\textquotedblright{} $\to$ Persian \textbf{dost}, and $\to$ English \textbf{choose}, \textbf{gusto}, \textbf{disgust}
  \item \emph{Sort:} \textbf{dost} Persian, \textbf{pāṇī} and \textbf{dudh} and \textbf{roṭī} Sanskrit-line
  \item \emph{Run through:} all four requests from last chapter, once more, for speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}friend.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Dost}.) What did its Persian root originally mean? (\textbf{To taste, to choose.}) Name two English words, from two different routes, that share that root. (\textbf{Choose}; \textbf{gusto} or \textbf{disgust}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%A6\%E0\%A9\%8B\%E0\%A8\%B8\%E0\%A8\%A4}{Wiktionary: \pa{ਦੋਸਤ}}; \href{https://www.etymonline.com/word/gusto}{Etymonline: gusto}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[parivār]{\pa{ਪਰਿਵਾਰ} — what surrounds you}

\label{lesson:PA-C11-parivar}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਦੋਸਤ}} (\emph{dost}) named one person, chosen. This word names the group you never chose at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਪਰਿਵਾਰ}} — \emph{parivār} — \textbf{family}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਪ}} \emph{p}, \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} \emph{r}, \textbf{\pa{ਿ}} short \emph{i}, \textbf{\pa{ਵ}} \emph{v} — the same \textbf{\pa{ਵ}} you read in \textbf{\pa{ਵੇਖਣਾ}} — \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} long \emph{ā}, \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} \emph{r} again. \emph{Pa-ri-vā-r}, four syllables, no new letter in any of them.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਪਰਿਵਾਰ}} comes straight from Sanskrit \textbf{parivāra}, and unlike \textbf{dost} or \textbf{roṭī}, this one splits cleanly into two working pieces: \textbf{pari-}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{around},\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{vṛ-}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to cover, to surround}.\textquotedblright{} A \emph{parivāra} is, word for word, what encloses you — the same \textbf{pari-} that opens \emph{parikramā}, a walk made \emph{around} something sacred, and a \textbf{vṛ-} that also sits inside \emph{varṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}covering\textquotedblright{} — the word Sanskrit used for both colour and social class.

Unlike \textbf{dost}, this is Sanskrit through and through. Unlike \textbf{roṭī}, its root is not a mystery — you can point at both halves and say what each one meant on its own.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{parivār} — family
  \item \emph{Split:} \textbf{pari-} \textquotedblleft{}around\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{vṛ-} \textquotedblleft{}to cover\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{parivār}
  \item \emph{Sort:} \textbf{dost} Persian, \textbf{roṭī} Sanskrit-but-unknown-root, \textbf{parivār} Sanskrit-and-transparent
  \item \emph{Name:} one other Sanskrit word built on \textbf{pari-} or \textbf{vṛ-}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}family.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Parivār}.) Split it into its two Sanskrit pieces and say what each meant. (\textbf{Pari-}, \textquotedblleft{}around\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{vṛ-}, \textquotedblleft{}to cover.\textquotedblright{}) Which of this chapter's two words so far has a root you can point at, and which does not? (\emph{Parivār} does; \emph{dost} is Persian, a different question entirely.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit/Hindi parivār}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bharā]{\pa{ਭਰਾ} — a breathy letter you have not met yet}

\label{lesson:PA-C11-bhara}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kòṛā} the horse dipped and rose because its old \textbf{\pa{ਘ}} lost its breath at the \textbf{start} of the word. This chapter's word does the same thing, with a different consonant, and it is not a verb this time — it is somebody you know.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਭਰਾ}} — \emph{bharā} — \textbf{brother}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਭ}} — new: the fourth letter of the \emph{p}-row, once \emph{bha}, a \emph{b} said with a breathy voice. Then \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} \emph{r}, \textbf{\pa{ਾ}} long \emph{ā}.

\begin{sounds}
Chapter 7 showed word-\textbf{initial} \textbf{\pa{ਘ}} losing its breath and leaving a low, rising pitch — \emph{kòṛā}. \textbf{\pa{ਭ}} is the same story with a different letter: said at the front of a word, its breath is gone too, and what is left is a plain, voiceless \textbf{p}, plus a \textbf{low} tone on the vowel after it.

\textbf{\pa{ਭਰਾ}} is therefore not said \emph{bharā}. It is said \textbf{prā̀} — \emph{p}, not \emph{bh}, and low on the first vowel. Spelling keeps the old consonant; speech keeps only its pitch.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{position in the word} & \textbf{old sound} & \textbf{what survives} \\
\midrule
initial (\emph{bh-}, \emph{gh-} …) & breathy voice & \textbf{low} tone, consonant plain \\
medial (\emph{-jh-}, \emph{-ḍh-} …) & breathy voice & \textbf{high, falling} tone \\
final, nothing after & any lost breath & \textbf{high, level} tone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three positions, three outcomes, and you have now met a word for each.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bharā} is inherited from Sanskrit \textbf{bhrātṛ}, root Indo-European *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}. This is one of the cleanest cognate sets in the family: Sanskrit \emph{bhrātṛ}, English \textbf{brother}, Latin \emph{frāter}, Greek \emph{phrātēr}, Russian \emph{brat} — every one of them the same word, by ordinary sound change, in every branch, no borrowing anywhere. Where \textbf{parivār} kept both its Sanskrit halves intact, \textbf{bharā} shows what centuries of everyday wear does instead: the whole cluster \emph{bhr-} thinned down to a single consonant and a tone.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{bharā} as it is said — \emph{prā̀}, low on the first vowel
  \item \emph{Trace it:} PIE \emph{b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr} $\to$ Sanskrit \emph{bhrātṛ} $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਭਰਾ}}, and $\to$ English \textbf{brother}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{bharā}, worn down to a tone, against \emph{parivār}, kept whole
  \item \emph{Run through:} the three-position tone table, one word for each row
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How is \textbf{\pa{ਭਰਾ}} actually said? (\emph{\textbf{Prā̀}} — \emph{p}, not \emph{bh}, low tone.) Which English word is the very same word, by unbroken descent? (\textbf{Brother}.) Name the three positions this book's tone rule now covers, and one word for each. (Initial — \emph{bharā}, low; medial — \emph{samajhṇā}, falling; final — \emph{cāh}, level high.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%AD\%E0\%A8\%B0\%E0\%A8\%BE}{Wiktionary: \pa{ਭਰਾ}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/b\%CA\%B0r\%C3\%A9h\%E2\%82\%82t\%C4\%93r}{Wiktionary: b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhaiṇ]{\pa{ਭੈਣ} — the same tone, a different family tree}

\label{lesson:PA-C11-bhain}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\pa{ਭਰਾ}} the way it is actually said — \emph{prā̀}, low. This chapter's last word starts with the same letter and the same tone. Whether it shares brother's family tree is a separate question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਭੈਣ}} — \emph{bhaiṇ} — \textbf{sister}
\end{quote}

Said \textbf{pàiṇ} — the same \textbf{\pa{ਭ} $\to$ p + low tone} shift as \textbf{\pa{ਭਰਾ}}, now on a different vowel, closed by the curled-back \textbf{\pa{ਣ}} you already read in \textbf{\pa{ਜਾਣਨਾ}}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਭ}} \emph{bh}, already yours from \emph{bharā} — the second word in this book to use it. \textbf{\pa{ੈ}} the \emph{ai}-sign, from \textbf{\pa{ਹੈ}}. \textbf{\pa{ਣ}} retroflex \emph{n}. Three letters, none of them new, and the tone is the same rule as last lesson, run again.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਭੈਣ}} is inherited from Sanskrit \textbf{bhaginī}, built on \textbf{bhaga-}, \textquotedblleft{}a share, a portion\textquotedblright{} — a sister, etymologically, as one who holds a share. That root is Indo-Aryan, not a straight PIE kinship term: the old Proto-Indo-European word for \textquotedblleft{}sister,\textquotedblright{} *\emph{swésōr}, is exactly what gives English \textbf{sister} — and Sanskrit simply stopped using it, replacing it with this one instead.

So \textbf{\pa{ਭਰਾ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਭੈਣ}} are not a matched pair the way English \emph{brother} and \emph{sister} feel like one. \emph{Bharā} is the unbroken PIE cousin of \emph{brother}. \emph{Bhaiṇ} is a homegrown Indo-Aryan replacement, unrelated in root to \emph{sister} — even though both now open with the identical \emph{bh-become-p-plus-low-tone} sound, purely by coincidence of which consonant each word once started with.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{bhaiṇ} as it is said — \emph{pàiṇ}, low tone
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{bharā} — true PIE cousin of \emph{brother}; \emph{bhaiṇ} — unrelated to \emph{sister}, despite the matching tone
  \item \emph{Run through:} all four people-words — \textbf{dost}, \textbf{parivār}, \textbf{bharā}, \textbf{bhaiṇ}
  \item \emph{Sort:} Persian (\textbf{dost}), Sanskrit-transparent (\textbf{parivār}), Sanskrit-cognate (\textbf{bharā}), Sanskrit-but-not-cognate (\textbf{bhaiṇ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}sister,\textquotedblright{} and how it is actually said. (\emph{Bhaiṇ}; \emph{pàiṇ}, low tone.) Is \emph{bhaiṇ} the same word as English \emph{sister}, the way \emph{bharā} is the same word as \emph{brother}? (\textbf{No} — Sanskrit replaced the old PIE sister-word with \emph{bhaginī}, \textquotedblleft{}a share-holder.\textquotedblright{}) Run this chapter's four people-words and what each one's history is. (\emph{Dost} Persian; \emph{parivār} Sanskrit and transparent; \emph{bharā} Sanskrit and an unbroken cousin; \emph{bhaiṇ} Sanskrit but not a cousin of \emph{sister}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%AD\%E0\%A9\%88\%E0\%A8\%A3}{Wiktionary: \pa{ਭੈਣ}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/sw\%C3\%A9s\%C5\%8Dr}{Wiktionary: swésōr}.
\end{tcolorbox}
